London’s community gardens: seven small spaces reclaimed by local people

These are not miniature parks. They are pieces of bombsite, railway land, alley and threatened open space made useful through local work and persistence.

By Paolo Pastorino12 October 20268 min read
At a glance
Admission
Free; cafés, donations and volunteering help keep the gardens open ↗
Access
Opening can change with staffing, weather, maintenance and events ↗
Allow
15–60 minutes per garden, depending on its size and programme
Photography
Avoid identifiable visitors and respect working plots

London’s smallest green spaces are easy to describe as ‘hidden gems’. The phrase is flattering but incomplete. A community garden is not valuable because tourists have failed to notice it. It matters because residents, volunteers and local organisations have taken responsibility for land that was neglected, damaged, threatened or simply missing from the public map.

The seven gardens below are very different. One fills a narrow cut-through near London Bridge; another occupies a former railway line; two grew from bomb-damaged ground. Some focus on food growing, others on wildlife, social programmes or the right to sit somewhere without paying. All depend on people and funding. Visit them as small pieces of social infrastructure, not as decorative backdrops. For more places and volunteering opportunities, use the Capital Growth network, which connects more than 2,000 food-growing spaces across London.

Gibbon’s Rent Secret Garden: an alley made generous

Gibbon’s Rent runs between Magdalen Street and Holyrood Street, close to London Bridge. Before its transformation in 2012, it was a long-overlooked cut-through. Architect Andrew Burns and landscape architect Sarah Eberle worked with Team London Bridge, the Architecture Foundation and Southwark Council to make it a container garden rather than erase the narrow character of the alley.

Rainwater harvesting supports a changing collection of indigenous and exotic plants contributed by local residents and businesses. A Little Library invites people to borrow or leave books. Those details make the project more than streetscape improvement: water, plants and books all circulate. Ten minutes is enough to see the space, but its real lesson is that a passage does not need to become a destination to become hospitable.

Official visitor information →

Culpeper Community Garden: a park shared through plots

Culpeper sits behind busy streets near Angel and Chapel Market. It works simultaneously as a public garden and an environmental community project. Paths move between a lawn, ponds, ornamental planting, wildlife areas and dozens of plots used by local people and groups, including gardeners who do not have outdoor space at home.

The result is neither a municipal park nor an allotment closed to outsiders. Private effort and public access overlap. Children gather around the pond, office workers use the lawn, volunteers work the beds and plot holders give the garden its constantly changing character. Culpeper is free and aims to open most days, but staffing and events can affect access. The right response to an unexpectedly closed gate is not indignation; it is to remember that a small charity is maintaining what looks effortless.

Official visitor information →

Calthorpe Community Garden: green space as a social programme

Calthorpe occupies a larger site near King’s Cross, yet its greatest value is not visual. For more than forty years it has used gardens, food growing, sport and creative activity to support health and connection. There are places to sit and grow, but also youth work, horticultural courses and a regular programme that makes the garden useful to different groups at different times.

This is what separates community space from passive landscaping. The ground hosts relationships as well as plants. Calthorpe welcomes casual visitors, but watch what is happening around the edges: raised beds, sports areas, volunteers and meeting spaces reveal an organisation designed around participation. Its position amid intense development also makes the continued presence of open, locally governed land especially significant.

Official visitor information →

The Hoxton Trust Community Garden: a garden attached to practical help

The Hoxton Trust maintains an unusually dense garden on Hoxton Street, an area where many residents live in flats without private outdoor space. Volunteers care for the trees, flowers, compost and habitat, while the garden hosts groups, events and informal daily use. Its planting is rich, but the organisational context is more revealing.

The Trust also provides free legal advice and supports local organisations. Garden and advice service may appear unrelated; in practice, both reduce isolation and give residents access to resources that would otherwise be difficult to obtain. If you continue towards Old Street, our article on Wesley’s Chapel and Bunhill Fields adds another layer of local social history, from religious dissent to reform and public burial space.

Official visitor information →

Dalston Eastern Curve Garden: a railway line that pays its own way

Dalston Eastern Curve Garden was created in 2010 on part of the former railway alignment that once linked Dalston Junction with the North London Line. Trees and dense planting now screen much of the surrounding city, while tables, children’s areas and a pavilion turn the long site into a shared outdoor room.

The café-bar is not an accessory. Its income funds the garden’s daily operation and helps keep entry free. Buying a drink therefore has a direct relationship to maintaining the space. Dalston is lively rather than silent, particularly at weekends and during events. Visit early for the plants; return later if you want to understand how the same garden becomes neighbourhood meeting place, family venue and social enterprise.

Official visitor information →

Bonnington Square Pleasure Garden: a bombsite turned subtropical room

Bonnington Square, near Vauxhall, was built for railway workers in the nineteenth century. Houses damaged during the Second World War left a central gap that later became a neglected playground and wasteland. Residents formed a garden association and, in the 1990s, transformed it into the Pleasure Garden—its name deliberately recalling the much larger Vauxhall Pleasure Gardens nearby.

The planting combines an English garden with an antipodean, almost subtropical character: palms, bamboo, a large walnut and layered foliage make the enclosure feel larger than it is. Industrial fragments and paths give it structure. The surrounding co-operative history matters as much as the plants. Residents did not merely beautify a leftover site; they extended planting into nearby streets and created a model of collective care maintained through volunteer workdays.

Official visitor information →

The Phoenix Garden: wildlife behind the West End

The Phoenix Garden occupies a former bombsite behind the Phoenix Theatre, between Soho and Covent Garden. Established in 1984, it has survived in an area where almost every square metre is under commercial pressure. Winding beds, a small pond and a pavilion create habitat for insects, birds and amphibians while giving West End workers and visitors somewhere quiet to pause.

Its central location can disguise the labour involved. The garden is a charity, supported by donations, friends and volunteers. Daily dawn-to-dusk opening is the standard pattern, but private events or maintenance can change access. The gate and hand-painted sign are part of its charm; the stronger achievement is that a site formed by destruction continues to serve wildlife and people four decades later.

Official visitor information →

How to use these spaces well

Do not try to collect all seven in one day. Build two compact walks: Gibbon’s Rent with Borough and Bermondsey; Culpeper and Calthorpe with the Regent’s Canal; Hoxton and Dalston as an east London pair; Bonnington with Vauxhall; Phoenix with Soho and Covent Garden. Check the organisation’s page before making a special journey, particularly in winter or when an event is scheduled.

Community gardens are free, but they are not costless. Use the café where one exists, donate, join a workday or share the official volunteer link. Keep to paths and public areas, avoid photographing identifiable garden users without permission, and do not treat food plots as flower displays. A short, respectful visit is more useful than turning a small local refuge into another crowded ‘secret London’ location.

What these gardens reclaim is not only land. They reclaim the possibility that a valuable London space can be managed for use, encounter and care rather than maximum financial return.
